_comment: The corpus tools/corpus-gen measures, as globs rather than a list of paths:
adding a configuration to the corpus should mean adding the configuration.
Origin is carried into live/corpus-refusals.json and is the field that
decides what a ranking over this corpus is worth. Configurations this
project wrote measure this project's own idea of what works; only
third-party ones measure the product promise, which is about
configurations nobody here wrote.
The terraform-aws-modules sources are pinned to an exact commit and
materialized by tools/corpus-fetch into .corpus/, which is gitignored.
They are the examples/ root modules each module ships - real, widely
deployed, and written by people who have never heard of live markers.
One caveat to hold while reading the ranking: module-author style leans
harder on variables, conditionals and dynamic blocks than an ordinary
estate does, so this corpus probably reports worse than typical user
code rather than better.
Each fetch block records both a tag and the commit it must resolve to.
corpus-fetch refuses a tag that has been moved, so the artifact cannot
silently change under an input nobody watched.
The published-deployment sources (#147) are whole deployment root
modules their operators published: each root describes one deployment,
not a module's option surface, which is what makes this the one
population whose blocked count may read as a compatibility rate
(reads_as: rate; see rateCapableOrigins). None of these repositories
tag releases, so they are pinned by commit alone and corpus-fetch
checks the commit out directly. Licenses checked 2026-08-15: MIT
(simpleinfra, govuk-aws, govuk-infrastructure, mastino,
cloud-platform-infrastructure), CC0-1.0 (both cisagov repos),
Apache-2.0 (k8s.io).
var_files and var_file_layout (#183, reworked to the parity ruling on
2026-08-15) run each estate the way its own operator does: with the
tfvars files the estate's own repository ships, discovered from its
own layout, never a value this project composed. A refusal that is
only an artifact of a required variable nobody supplied a value for is
flagged unset_var_only in live/corpus-refusals.json (#178's rule-2
scoping); supplying the estate's own file is how that gets told apart
from a real language-wall blocker, honestly, rather than papered over.
var_file_layout derives var files from a directory's own name, for a
layout expressible as a rule - see [ManifestSource.VarFileLayout]'s
doc comment. Of the four corpus repositories that ship any tfvars:
- govuk-infrastructure uses it: terraform/deployments/<name> pairs
with terraform/variables/<env>/<name>.tfvars plus that env's own
common.tfvars, both applied when the estate ships them. Which env:
"integration" is picked uniformly (not per estate) because it has
the widest coverage among the four - 25 of the 35 in-corpus
deployments ship an integration/<name>.tfvars, against 24 for
production, 23 for staging and 1 for test.
- mastino needs no entry at all: every tfvars file it ships is a
*.auto.tfvars sitting in the same directory as the deployment it
configures, which internal/live/check's loader already reads from
the measured directory itself, with no manifest wiring, exactly as
stock OpenTofu auto-loads it.
- k8s.io ships terraform.tfvars for two in-corpus projects
(cdn.packages.k8s.io, prow-build-cluster), also auto-loaded with no
entry needed. Three others (artifacts.k8s.io, kops-infra-ci, macos)
ship only atlantis.tfvars, applied by an Atlantis workflow named
"aws" in the repo's .atlantis.yaml - but that workflow's own
extra_args (whether it actually passes -var-file=atlantis.tfvars)
live in Atlantis server config, not in the repository, so this
manifest does not wire them: doing so would be inferring CI
plumbing this project cannot read, not reading a file the estate
unambiguously ships as its own input.
- cloud-platform-infrastructure ships 6 tfvars files, all under
aws-accounts/<account>/{account,vpc/eks,...}, one or two directory
levels below the account directory this manifest's glob matches;
the account directory itself (and global-resources, the only other
in-corpus entry) has no .tf files directly, so HasConfigFiles
excludes it and neither in-corpus entry has a tfvars file of its
own to apply. Reaching the nested root modules would mean widening
the glob that decides which directories are in the corpus at all -
a different axis from var_files, not this change's to make.
- govuk-aws ships zero tfvars files anywhere in the repository; its
estates stay language-blocked on unset_var_only refusals, honestly,
with no entry here.
_module_sources_comment: Every git repository a corpus module call reaches through go-getter,
pinned to a commit. corpus-fetch mirrors each one under
.corpus/_modules and points git's url.<base>.insteadOf at the mirror
for the duration of the module install, so a source written as
github.com/org/repo installs from a frozen commit instead of whatever
that repository's default branch holds today. Without this the corpus
floated: counted on 2026-08-16 by walking each resolved entry through
its local module sources, 135 of its 284 non-local module calls are
go-getter sources and 134 of those carry no ?ref= at all.
Six of these seven are named by a corpus entry directly. The seventh,
cisagov/s3-read-role-tf-module, is reached only from inside another
go-getter module, which is why a census of the corpus's own .tf files
does not find it and why corpus-fetch reports unpinned repositories
from the records the installer actually wrote.
repo is the clone URL go-getter hands to git, which is the .git
spelling. That suffix is load-bearing and not cosmetic: the OpenTofu
registry serves module downloads as
git::https://github.com/<org>/<repo>?ref=<commit> with no .git, so
keying the rewrite on the .git spelling leaves every registry install
untouched. See tools/corpus-fetch/gitmirror.go.
commit is the repository's default-branch head at the moment the pin
was taken (2026-08-16), which is what an unpinned run would have
installed that day. The ref names each mirror serves are recorded
separately in live/corpus-module-pins.json, which corpus-fetch writes.
A go-getter call whose repository is not listed here is reported by
corpus-fetch and has its module record dropped, so it stays as
unresolved as it was before module installation existed rather than
silently floating into a measurement.
